planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall into well-drained soil in full sun; give it room to develop its broad, irregular crown and avoid any site with standing water.

directions: Guadalupe Cypress is a Baja California island endemic valued in cultivation for its handsome blue-gray to blue-green foliage and thick, fibrous reddish bark, qualities that have made it a sought-after specimen tree in Mediterranean-climate gardens and arboreta. It grows into a broad, irregularly pyramidal tree and tolerates salt spray, wind, and extended drought once its roots are established, but like its Monterey Cypress relatives it fails quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil. Because wild populations on Guadalupe Island have been decimated by feral goat grazing, cultivated specimens in botanic gardens and private collections now represent an important conservation resource for the species. Give young trees full sun and only occasional supplemental water beyond their first year or two.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container nursery stock in spring into well-drained soil; seed has a deep double dormancy and is rarely practical for home propagation.

directions: Japanese Hophornbeam is a tough, adaptable East Asian shade tree closely related to the American hophornbeam, distinguished by its shaggy, flaking gray-brown bark and pendulous clusters of papery, hop-like fruiting bracts that persist into fall. It tolerates a wide range of soils, including dry or compacted sites, and develops a tidy rounded crown with clean yellow autumn color. Growth is slow to moderate, so plant it where its long-term structure and interesting bark texture can be appreciated from a nearby path or patio. It transplants best as younger nursery stock, since older specimens resent root disturbance.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall as rains return, siting it in shaded or partly shaded ground with reliable moisture; the extremely pliable stems and bark resent rough handling during planting.

directions: Western Leatherwood is a rare California endemic shrub confined to shaded canyons and north-facing slopes around the San Francisco Bay Area, where it is among the earliest native shrubs to flower, opening small pale-yellow bells on bare stems in midwinter well before the leaves emerge. Its bark and twigs are remarkably tough yet flexible, a trait early settlers exploited for cordage and that gives the plant its common name. In the garden it performs best as a woodland understory specimen with consistent moisture, filtered light, and rich, humus-laden soil similar to the shaded ravines where it grows wild. It is slow-growing and long-lived, and once sited well it needs little routine care beyond protecting it from summer drought stress.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in a site sheltered from strong wind.

directions: Chinese Yellowwood is a graceful relative of the better-known American yellowwood, native to central China, with smooth gray bark, pinnately compound leaves that emerge coppery-pink in spring, and loose panicles of fragrant, pale pink-flushed white pea-like flowers in early summer. It tends to flower at a younger age and more dependably from year to year than its American counterpart, making it a rewarding specimen for arboreta and larger home landscapes. The wood is brittle at branch unions, so structural pruning while the tree is young helps prevent storm damage later on. It adapts to a range of soils as long as drainage is good and appreciates a site with full sun and shelter from desiccating winds.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; seed has a double dormancy requiring warm then cold stratification and is slow and uneven to germinate.

directions: Japanese Bladdernut is a compact East Asian shrub in the same genus as the native American bladdernut, bearing trifoliate leaves and upright clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by the inflated, papery, bladder-like seed capsules that give the genus its common name. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than its American or European relatives, making it a good choice for a woodland-edge border or mixed shrub planting where space is limited. It prefers cool, moist, humus-rich soil and benefits from light shade during the hottest part of the day in warmer parts of its range. The decorative seed pods persist into fall and add textural interest after the flowers have finished.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring into lean, rocky, fast-draining soil on a sunny slope or among stones.

directions: Rock Spray is a low, densely branched shrub of rocky slopes and canyon walls across the southwestern mountains, from Arizona and New Mexico north into Utah and Colorado, where its tiny, deeply lobed leaves and wiry stems form tight, drought-tolerant mounds among the stones. In summer it produces small plumes of creamy-white flowers that are noticeably finer and more compact than those of the coastal Oceanspray, reflecting its adaptation to drier, more exposed sites. It is an excellent choice for rock gardens, dry slopes, and xeriscape plantings in its native elevation range, needing almost no supplemental water once its roots are established among well-drained, mineral soil. Light, infrequent pruning after bloom keeps the mounded habit tidy without sacrificing next year's flowers.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
